title: Windsor Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Windsor wells have a 30 ft median depth, 30 gpm median reported yield, and estimated finished costs of $7,000-$13,600.
h1: What Windsor Well Records Mean for a Rural Property
intro_html:
Windsor sits on the plains, and the well records near town reflect that setting. Among 1,835 Colorado DWR permits in the local area, 1,033 are recorded as constructed. Reported depths are usually shallow, but the records also include a few much deeper wells. Reported production is generally strong, although only 180 wells list a pump yield and 140 list a static water level.

For a buyer, the useful takeaway is not one guaranteed depth or flow rate. It is the pattern: shallow alluvial and plains-sediment wells are common around Windsor, water levels are close to the surface, and a lot still needs to be checked individually before you rely on it for a house, livestock, or irrigation.

sections.heading: Windsor wells are usually shallow, but the spread matters
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Windsor is 30 feet. The middle half runs from 21 to 38 feet, and 93% of wells are under 100 feet. That is a favorable starting point for a drilling estimate in this plains setting. It does not mean every lot will match the median: the deepest record reaches 1,170 feet, while 3% of wells fall in each of the 100-to-300-foot and 300-to-600-foot ranges.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium wells also present. A driller should review nearby completion records, geology, and the intended use before firming up a bid. A shallow median supports a narrower initial estimate, but unusual ground conditions can change the hole depth quickly.

sections.heading: Reported Windsor yields are generally strong
sections.html:
Among the 180 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 30.0 gallons per minute. The middle half spans 15.0 to 200.0 gallons per minute, and 78% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, while another 1% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That is encouraging for a normal household well, but the yield figures are not a promise for an unbuilt lot. A test result, pump setting, storage tank, and the well's permitted use all matter. An exempt household-use well is subject to the state's 35 gpm pumping limit. Irrigation and other uses may require different permitting or water-right arrangements, especially in a basin where augmentation is required.

sections.heading: Windsor water levels look close to the surface
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median of 10 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 8 and 16 feet. That shallow water level fits the local plains and alluvial setting and can simplify initial drilling expectations. It can also mean that surface activities, poor casing, or damaged well seals deserve close attention.

The decade comparison does not show a clear dropping trend in these records: the median was 10 feet below surface in the 2010s and 9 feet in the 2020s. Treat that as a local record pattern, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. Static levels vary with location, season, pumping, and measurement quality. Ask for the well's construction report and recent performance information instead of relying only on the area median.

sections.heading: Windsor has a long permit and drilling history
sections.html:
Weld County records show permits from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The largest decade totals were 288 permits in the 2000s, 261 in the 2010s, and 240 in the 2020s. That history gives a buyer more neighboring records to compare, particularly around Windsor, Severance, and the edges toward Timnath.

The most active drillers in the available records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 403 wells, Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed) with 219, and R & R Well & Pump Inc. (Rank, Samuel C) with 74. Those names describe permit history, not an endorsement or a current bid. Confirm licensing, insurance, scope, and who will perform the work on your property.

sections.heading: A Windsor well budget starts near the shallow median
sections.html:
For Windsor's alluvium and plains sedimentary ground, the local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. Applied to the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,000 to $1,600. That is only the hole, not a functioning water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $7,000 to $13,600 at that median depth. The actual proposal can move outside that range if the hole is deeper, the site has difficult access, the pump must be set differently, or electrical and trenching runs are long. Get a written bid that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, electrical, and site restoration.

sections.heading: Check water quality, low-yield risk, and the building site
sections.html:
Depth and flow are only part of the due diligence. Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 655 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 2 historic mine features. These records do not prove a problem at a specific lot, but they justify testing the existing well and checking the property's location against known sites.

Have the well tested for the contaminants relevant to the area and the property's history. Confirm casing, grout, well cap, pump condition, and separation from septic components. Before building, verify the permit allows the planned use, identify the septic area and replacement area, and confirm access for a drill rig. A low-yield or dry hole is uncommon in the reported yield mix, but neighboring records cannot eliminate parcel-level risk.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Windsor, Colorado?
faq.a: Windsor well records show a median reported depth of 30 feet. The middle half runs from 21 to 38 feet, and 93% are under 100 feet. The range is not uniform: the deepest recorded well is 1,170 feet. Use nearby completion reports and a driller's site review to estimate the depth for a specific parcel.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Windsor?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $35 to $55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary ground. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,000 to $1,600. A finished system including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $7,000 to $13,600. A deeper or difficult site can cost more.

faq.q: How much water do Windsor wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 180 local wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 30.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 200.0 gallons per minute, and 78% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These figures describe recorded wells, not a guarantee. Test the specific well and confirm its permitted use before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Windsor?
faq.a: A well's safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Local records include 655 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with EPA cleanup sites and historic mine features. Test an existing well for relevant contaminants, review its construction and location, and retest after ownership or property conditions change.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Windsor?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a clear decline. Reported static water levels were 10 feet below surface in the 2010s and 9 feet in the 2020s. The data cover only 140 wells with reported static levels, so they should not replace a current measurement. Seasonal conditions, pumping, and the individual aquifer still matter.
